translations: Lü Dongbin wasn’t about to be outshone. He drew his emerald‑glow sword, and in the sunset its blade flashed a rainbow halo. With a single slash he sliced the sea, the tip of his sword skimming the crest of a wave and actually cleaving the wave in two, revealing a clear water channel. The strike sent a spray of mist up like a knife‑cut splash, and within the mist a faint golden‑scaled fish silhouette flickered, making Lü stumble back a half‑step and exclaim, “Even the fish wants to steal my spotlight!”

Seeing this, He Xiangu lifted her hand lightly, snapped her fingers, and the embroidered fan in her grasp unfurled, its surface painted with swirling clouds. With a gentle flick, the sea breeze was sucked into the fan, forming a soft current that pushed the wave back. She laughed, “This fan isn’t for swatting mosquitoes—it’s for taming unruly waves.”

Lan Caihe saw the sparks from his golden hoop staff wobble in the wind, grabbed it hard, and the staff began to hum like it was charged with electricity. He shouted in surprise, “The staff can charge itself!” Then he hoisted it high, pointing the tip at the sea. A beam of golden light shot into the water, and the surface instantly bubbled with tiny fizzing bubbles, as if soda had been ignited.

Han Xiangzi pulled out his tiny jade flute and played a lilting “Qing Ping Diao.” The melody floated over the water, soothing the frothy waves until they calmed, as if they’d heard a mother’s lullaby and settled down.
Iron‑Cane Li slipped the gourd from his shoulder and weighed it in his palm. “Since we’re all waiting, someone’s got to go first,” he said.
Han Zhongli called out, “Take it slow. My fan’s mood is still a mystery today.”
Iron‑Cane Li hummed, stepped to the front. The other seven didn’t intervene, just cleared a space. The first magical treasure of the Eight Immortals was about to leave the shore.
Iron‑Cane Li popped the gourd’s stopper, gave it a sniff to make sure it wasn’t last night’s leftover wine, then tossed the gourd toward the sea.

The gourd swelled in the wind, landed on a wave and steadied a patch of shimmering water. Iron‑Cane Li planted his iron cane and hopped on. Just as he was about to turn and say, “Watch this,” the gourd spun half a turn, pointing him back toward the shore.
Zhang Guolao called from behind, “Is this a departure or a return?”

Ignoring him, Iron‑Cane Li used his cane to tap the water, trying to set the direction right. The gourd obediently spun another half‑turn. This time the heading was correct, but the next wave pushed him right back where he started.
Lan Caihe chuckled, “Steady progress—just not moving at all.”

“Shut up,” Iron‑Cane Li snapped, laying his cane across his side. When a wave came, he used it to skim the water and catch the surge. The gourd finally slipped past the near‑shore breakers and slid outward. A side gust, however, made its path wobble like a snake that’d forgotten its brain.
Han Zhongli saw this and stepped forward, unfurling his banana leaf fan. “Let me give you a ride.”

He tried to push the wind behind the gourd, but his first gust was too strong. Sand and dust rose from the shore, the sea’s crest fell forward, and Iron‑Cane Li, gourd and all, shot out wildly, then spun in the wind’s wake.
“Are you sending me across the sea,” Iron‑Cane Li shouted from a distance, “or just to the edge of the ocean?”
Han Zhongli quickly folded his fan. Zhang Guolao, standing nearby, offered a serious comment, “Make it bigger and you could send him back to yesterday.”

Iron‑Cane Li pressed his iron cane against one side of the gourd, finally stopping its spin. He didn’t brag about not needing help; he just gestured toward the shore with his cane, “Gentle wind, come from behind my back.”

Han Zhongli first tried sending a single gust. The gourd moved forward but was nudged off course by a wave. Iron‑Cane Li didn’t push him to add more force; he simply nudged the gourd back with his cane. One adjusted the wind, the other set the heading. After a few tries they found a rhythm where neither had to scramble to fix the other.

Han Zhongli stopped treating his fan like a broom. He watched the sea’s wind pattern and gave a light flick. The breeze from behind the gourd pushed it gently—no tugging, no rush. Riding the gourd, Iron‑Cane Li grew steadier; his cane tapped the water now and then, letting him dodge oncoming waves.
Once the gourd steadied, Iron‑Cane Li complained, “If you’d fanned like that earlier, I wouldn’t have spun so many times.”
Han Zhongli replied, “If you hadn’t spun those extra circles, I’d have no idea which way to fan.”
“So it’s still my credit after all.”
“Take the credit if you want, just don’t bring the circles back with you.”

When they reached farther out at sea, Han Zhongli took a step forward. The banana leaf fan unfolded in his hand, and the wind it generated lifted his robes and his feet. He walked on the breeze he created, each flap carrying him over another wave.
Iron‑Cane Li looked back and deliberately said, “Your route looks comfy.”
Han Zhongli answered, “I tried you out earlier, so of course it’s comfortable.”
“You admit you used me as a test fan?”
“I only admit you turned out pretty useful.”

Their voices were carried back to shore by the sea breeze, and the remaining six immortals burst into laughter. Amid the chuckles, Iron‑Cane Li’s gourd kept rolling, Han Zhongli’s fan stayed steady. One steadied the path with a cane, the other rode on a gentle wind—each crossing the choppiest near‑shore water in their own style.
